Them Optimally
Verbockhaven et al. | TMLR 2024
This fixture captures a real paper on growing small networks during training.
The method detects expressivity bottlenecks from backpropagation signals and
adds neurons where the current architecture cannot follow the functional gradient.
The paper reports CIFAR results that match larger models with less manual search.

provider_result.raw_text:
Growing Tiny Networks: Spotting Expressivity Bottlenecks and Fixing
Them Optimally
Verbockhaven et al. | TMLR 2024
This fixture captures a real paper on growing small networks during training.
The method detects expressivity bottlenecks from backpropagation signals and
adds neurons where the current architecture cannot follow the functional gradient.
The paper reports CIFAR results that match larger models with less manual search.
provider_result.title: growing-tiny-networks-2024

claims: Expressivity bottlenecks can be identified from backpropagation‑derived functional gradient mismatches.
Adding neurons at detected bottlenecks improves the network's ability to follow the functional gradient.
The resulting grown tiny networks achieve accuracy on par with larger, hand‑tuned architectures.
findings: CIFAR‑10/100 results match those of larger baseline models while requiring fewer manual design choices.
mechanistic_notes: Bottleneck detection relies on comparing the desired functional gradient with the current network's Jacobian‑vector product.
New neurons are inserted in parallel to existing units, receiving the same incoming weights and initialized to break symmetry.
The growth step is performed intermittently during training, allowing the optimizer to re‑converge after each insertion.
open_questions: How does the method scale to deeper architectures or larger datasets beyond CIFAR?
What is the optimal frequency and magnitude for neuron insertion to avoid instability?
